prime.problem: Insertion sort's one-swap-per-inversion is O(n²) on random data. To get n log n in place, you need a single sweep that settles one element for good and splits the rest into independent halves. How evenly it splits decides everything.
prime.fits: Second sort. Insertion sort showed the cost of fixing order locally; quicksort fixes it globally with a partition. Quickselect reuses the partition next, and heapsort appears here as introsort's fallback.
expect: pivot lands in its final place
worst case n(n − 1)/2 on sorted input
prime.goal: Trace a Lomuto partition, predict when quicksort degrades to n², and choose the pivot rule and stack order that prevent it.

attend: After one partition, which single element is guaranteed to be in its final sorted position, and why?
Why does a last-element pivot on already-sorted input peel off just one element per partition?
Why does pushing the larger range first cap the stack at O(log n), while the source's left-then-right order can hold 1,001 ranges?
Why isn't quicksort stable, even though Lomuto only ever swaps forward?
What does introsort switch to, and at what recursion depth?

must: One sweep puts everything < pivot left and the rest right → the pivot sits at its sorted index → the two sides are independent subproblems → about n compares per level

Split quality sets the depth → balanced splits give ≈ log n levels (≈ 2n ln n ≈ 1.39 n log₂ n compares, 24,785,482 for 10⁶) → an extreme pivot every time gives n levels → n(n − 1)/2 (28 for sorted n = 8; 499,999,500,000 for 10⁶)

Sorted, reversed and all-equal inputs are common and an attacker can craft them → fixed pivots are unsafe → random or median-of-3 pivot, a 3-way partition for duplicates, and introsort's heapsort fallback past ≈ 2 log₂ n depth give an O(n log n) guarantee
elevated: Process the smaller range first (push the larger one first) → every waiting range is at most half its parent → the stack holds O(log n) ranges instead of O(n) (2 vs 1,001 on reversed n = 2,000)
Partition scans memory sequentially and sorts in place → cache-friendly → why introsort (0.031 s) beats numpy's stable sort (0.072 s) on 10⁶ floats
reference: the 4.2× sorted() vs np.sort split being mostly object overhead

compress.prompt: Draw quicksort as a chain from memory: pick pivot → partition → pivot fixed → two subranges → stack. Then add one branch for "balanced split" and one for "extreme pivot", each ending in its compare count, and one line on how introsort guards the bad branch.
checklist: one partition sweep costs about the range size in compares
the pivot lands at its final index; the sides never mix again
balanced splits → log n levels → n log n; extreme pivots → n levels → n²
sorted input with a last-element pivot is the classic worst case
random or median-of-3 pivot, 3-way partition, heapsort fallback
in place, O(log n) stack if the smaller side goes first; not stable

retrieve.q: Explain why a pivot that always lands at an end of its range turns quicksort into an O(n²) algorithm, in terms of levels and work per level.
answer: each partition removes only the pivot, leaving n − 1 elements
so there are n levels instead of log n
work per level is still about the range size: (n − 1) + (n − 2) + … = n(n − 1)/2

retrieve.q: Walk through the Lomuto partition of a with pivot 10: what i tracks, which elements get swapped, and where 10 ends up.
answer: i marks the end of the < pivot region, starting at lo − 1
38, 27, 43 are not < 10; 3 (j = 3) and 9 (j = 4) are, so they swap to indices 0 and 1
82 is not; finally swap a[i + 1] with a[hi]: 10 lands at index 2
6 compares, 2 swaps, then 1 final placement swap

retrieve.q: You're sorting 10⁶ user records by signup date, and ties must keep the order they were fetched in. Is quicksort the right call? What would you use instead, and what does it cost?
answer: no: quicksort is not stable, so ties get reordered
use a stable sort: sorted()/Timsort or merge sort
cost: an O(n) buffer, and numpy's stable sort was 2.3× slower than introsort on floats

compare.q: Quicksort splits then does nothing to combine; merge sort splits trivially then merges. Where does each put its work, which design choice makes merge sort's cost input-independent, and how does each fail?
answer: quicksort's work is the partition before recursing; merge sort's is the merge after
merge sort always splits in the middle, so depth is always log₂ n
quicksort fails on bad pivots (n²) and isn't stable; merge sort needs an n-element buffer and is slower in memory

compare.q: Introsort runs quicksort and falls back to heapsort. What does each contribute, and why not run heapsort from the start?
answer: quicksort: fast sequential sweeps, in place, fastest on average
heapsort: O(n log n) on every input, in place
heapsort alone is slower (0.096 s vs 0.031 s for 10⁶ floats) because its parent–child jumps miss the cache
so heapsort is only the safety net when depth passes ≈ 2 log₂ n

predict.q: Run the card's Lomuto quicksort (last-element pivot) on 8 equal values, [5] × 8. How many compares, and why? What one change to the partition fixes it?
predict.answer: 28, the same as sorted input. Every a[j] < 5 test is false, so everything goes to the right side and the pivot lands at the end: each partition peels off one element. A 3-way partition (less / equal / greater) puts all the 5s in the middle in one pass and finishes immediately.

apply.task: Partition [9, 3, 7, 1, 8, 5] by hand with Lomuto and pivot 5: write the array after each swap, the final index of 5, and the compare count. Then finish the sort using the card's stack rule (smaller side first) and total the compares.
apply.done: After the first partition the array is [3, 1, 5, 9, 8, 7] with 5 at index 2 after 5 compares, and the whole sort takes 9 compares.
apply.hint: The left range [3, 1] costs 1 compare; the right range [9, 8, 7] costs 2 and leaves [7, 8, 9], so [8, 9] is still left to partition.
